text: Erasure is one of several rights an individual, a data subject, can invoke over their own personal data. This lesson covers the full set, and the process most organizations use to fulfill any of them.
Access, a copy of the personal data an organization holds. Rectification, correcting inaccurate or incomplete data. Erasure, deletion, under last lesson's conditions.

Portability, receiving data in a structured, commonly-used format to move to another provider. Restriction, limiting how data is processed without necessarily deleting it. Objection, opting out of specific processing, like certain marketing uses. Treating any request about someone's data as one generic bucket is a mistake, access and portability expect genuinely different outputs.

Most organizations run the same four steps regardless of which right is invoked. Verify identity first, skipping this turns the privacy right into an attack vector, an impersonator requesting someone else's data is a real risk. Locate the data, every system that holds it, not just the obvious one. Compile and respond, an export, a correction, a deletion confirmation, within the response window. Log the request, what was asked, when, what was done, independent of the underlying data.

Locating the data is usually where this breaks down in practice. Personal data about one person is rarely in one table, it's scattered across the application database, a data warehouse copy, a CRM, a support tool, email marketing, log files, sometimes unsanctioned spreadsheets. A credible process depends on already knowing where personal data lives, which is exactly what classification and a documented data inventory make possible.
Without that groundwork, every request becomes an improvised search. Next up: auditing and logging, the record-keeping layer that makes all of this demonstrable.
